title: RF exposure rules and evaluation
blurb: Explain how RF affects the body, who must evaluate exposure, and how to bring a station into compliance.

G0A01.why: RF is non-ionizing: its effect on tissue is **heating**.
G0A01.trap: RF doesn't cause radiation poisoning or change blood counts.

G0A02.why: Exposure depends on **duty cycle, frequency and power density**: every one of them is used.

G0A03.why: Calculation (OET Bulletin 65), computer modeling and calibrated measurement are **all accepted** ways to show compliance.

G0A04.why: Time averaging is the **total RF exposure averaged over a set period**, not the peak at one instant.

G0A05.why: If limits are exceeded, **take action to prevent human exposure**. No filing or neighbor permission is required.
G0A05.trap: There is no EIS-97 form, and neighbors can't waive limits.

G0A06.why: Failing the exemption criteria means you must **evaluate exposure per OET Bulletin 65**.

G0A07.why: Average exposure = power × duty cycle. **Lower duty cycle permits more power**. Nobody is exempt for either.
G0A07.trap: Higher duty cycle raises the average, so it permits less power.

G0A08.why: You must **routinely evaluate exposure and keep people away from high-exposure areas**. Posting or notifying neighbors isn't required.

G0A09.why: Only a **calibrated field strength meter with a calibrated antenna** measures field strength accurately.
G0A09.trap: SWR meters and receivers aren't calibrated for field strength.

G0A10.why: The fix is control: **make sure the antenna cannot point at them** when they are there.
G0A10.trap: Changing gain or front-to-back ratio doesn't remove the main lobe.

G0A11.why: An indoor antenna puts the field near people, so **make sure MPE limits aren't exceeded in occupied areas**.

G0A12.why: The rules cover **every station transmitting more than 1 mW time-averaged**. Amateur stations are not exempt.
